doc.title: Hide Tanaka interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 3, 2014

title: Falling for the acoustic bass and learning jazz by transcribing
summary: Tired of rock as performance, he heard acoustic bass in a Japanese jazz club, fell in love, studied with a private teacher and transcribed records.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: So you went from rock & roll to jazz music. And how did that happen?

You know, like after I was listening to rock music I was getting tired. It’s the same kind of thing. And rock music is more like a performance. Not just practice the instrument. I really wanted to play the instrument, not much like a performer you know, “hi everybody.” I’m not that kind of person. So sometimes I went to a Japanese jazz club with my friends, and I was just curious, you know, what is jazz. And the first time I heard acoustic bass I fell in love. I don’t know who was playing, I don’t care who was playing, I liked this acoustic bass sound. Then just jazz music was at that time — already rock music was using the acoustic bass. And okay, I should play jazz music. I started to get curious, what is jazz music. And after I heard about improvisation, you can change everything you know, and improvise. I really loved the way, how to construct jazz music. And that’s why this is my stuff.
How did you go about learning it?
I had a private teacher, a jazz bass player. And he also taught me classical etudes.
Was it something you could get on the radio?
Not on the radio, from the records. I bought a lot of the jazz records and transcribed myself.
Yeah. And sometimes, you know, like any other instrument, for my solo. The solo and bass playing, it’s different.
Yeah, I transcribed from many bass solos too. But I transcribed guitar players or horn players, a trumpet player.
